In mathematics, especially in the area of [[abstract algebra]], every [[Module (mathematics)|module]] has an associated '''character module'''. Using the associated character module it is possible to investigate the properties of the original module. One of the main results discovered by [[Joachim Lambek]] shows that a module is [[Flat module|flat]] [[if and only if]] the associated character module is [[Injective module|injective]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Lambek|first=Joachim|date=1964|title=A Module is Flat if and Only if its Character Module is Injective|journal=[[Canadian Mathematical Bulletin]]|language=en|volume=7|issue=2|pages=237–243|doi=10.4153/CMB-1964-021-9|issn=0008-4395|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Definition ==

The [[Group (mathematics)|group]] <math>(\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}, +)</math>, the group of rational numbers modulo <math display="inline">1</math>, can be considered as a <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-module in the natural way. Let <math>M</math> be an additive group which is also considered as a <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-module. Then the group <math display="block">M^* = \operatorname{Hom}_\mathbb{Z} (M, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z})</math> of <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-[[Module homomorphism|homomorphisms]] from <math>M</math> to <math>\mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}</math> is called the ''character group associated to <math>M</math>''. The elements in this group are called ''characters''. If <math>M</math> is a left <math>R</math>-module over a ring <math>R</math>, then the [[character group]] <math>M^*</math> is a right <math>R</math>-module and called the ''character module associated to'' <math>M</math>. The module action in the character module for <math>f \in \operatorname{Hom}_\mathbb{Z} (M, \mathbb{Q} / \mathbb{Z}) </math> and <math>r \in R </math> is defined by <math>(f r)(m) = f(rm)  </math> for all <math>m \in M</math>.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|title=Lectures on rings and modules|last=Lambek, Joachim.|date=2009|publisher=AMS Chelsea Pub|others=American Mathematical Society.|isbn=9780821849002|location=Providence, RI|oclc=838801039}}</ref> The character module can also be defined in the same way for right <math>R</math>-modules. In the literature also the notations <math>M', M^0</math> and <math>M^+</math> are used for character modules.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Lectures on Modules and Rings|last=Lam|first=Tsit-Yuen|author-link=Tsit Yuen Lam|date=1999|publisher=Springer New York|series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics|volume=189|location=New York, NY}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title=Module theory, extending modules and generalizations|last1=Tercan|first1=Adnan|last2=Yücel|first2=Canan C.|publisher=Birkhäuser|year=2016|isbn=9783034809528|series=Frontiers in Mathematics|location=Switzerland}}</ref> 

Let <math>M,N</math> be left <math>R</math>-modules and <math>f \colon M \to N</math> an <math>R</math>-homomorphism. Then the mapping <math>f^* \colon N^* \to M^*</math> defined by <math>f^* (h) = h \circ f</math> for all <math>h \in N^*</math> is a right <math>R</math>-homomorphism. Character module formation is a contravariant [[functor]] from the [[Category of modules|category]] of left <math>R</math>-modules to the category of right <math>R</math>-modules.<ref name=":0" />

== Motivation ==
The abelian group <math>\Q / \Z</math> is [[Divisible group|divisible]] and therefore an [[Injective module|injective]] <math>\Z</math>-module. Furthermore it has the following important property: Let <math>G</math> be an [[abelian group]] and <math>g \in G</math> nonzero. Then there exists a [[group homomorphism]] <math>f \colon G \to \Q / \Z</math> with <math>f(g) \neq 0</math>. This says that <math>\Q / \Z</math> is a [[Injective cogenerator|cogenerator]]. With these properties one can show the main theorem of the theory of character modules:<ref name=":0" /> <blockquote>'''Theorem (Lambek)'''<ref name=":1" />''':''' A left module <math>M</math> over a ring <math>R</math> is [[Flat module|flat]] if and only if the character module <math>M^*</math> is an [[Injective module|injective]] right <math>R</math>-module. </blockquote>

== Properties ==
Let <math>M</math> be a left module over a ring <math>R</math> and <math>M^*</math> the associated character module. 

* The module <math>M</math> is flat if and only if <math>M^*</math> is injective (Lambek's Theorem<ref name=":3" />).<ref name=":1" />
* If <math>M</math> is free, then <math>M^*</math> is an injective right <math>R</math>-module and <math>M^*</math> is a direct product of copies of the right <math>R</math>-modules <math>R^*</math>.<ref name=":2" />
*For every right <math>R</math>-module <math>N</math> there is a free module <math>M</math> such that <math>N</math> is isomorphic to a submodule of <math>M^*</math>. With the previous property this module <math>M^*</math> is injective, hence every right <math>R</math>-module is isomorphic to a submodule of an injective module. (Baer's Theorem)<ref name=":4">{{Cite book|title=Ring theory|last=Behrens, Ernst-August.|date=1972|publisher=Academic Press|isbn=9780080873572|location=New York|oclc=316568566}}</ref>
*A left <math>R</math>-module <math>N</math> is injective if and only if there exists a free <math>M</math> such that <math>N</math> is isomorphic to a direct summand of <math>M^*</math>.<ref name=":4" />
* The module <math>M</math> is injective if and only if it is a direct summand of a character module of a [[free module]].<ref name=":2" />
* If <math>N</math> is a submodule of <math>M</math>, then <math>(M/N)^*</math> is isomorphic to the submodule of <math>M^*</math> which consists of all elements which annihilate <math>N</math>.<ref name=":2" />
*Character module formation is a contravariant [[exact functor]], i.e. it preserves exact sequences.<ref name=":0" />
*Let <math>N</math> be a right <math>R</math>-module. Then the modules <math>\operatorname{Hom}_R (N, M^*)</math> and <math>(N \otimes_R M)^*</math> are isomorphic as <math>\Z</math>-modules.<ref name=":3" />
